analysis.one_liner: Cuts mercury pollution 90% from coal-fired power plants and phases out mercury in consumer products.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: introduced in August 2001, it sat in the House Energy and Commerce Committee and its energy subcommittee until the Congress ended in January 2003.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required coal- and oil-fired power plants and large industrial boilers to cut their mercury emissions by at least 90%, and chlor-alkali and cement plants by 95%. It would also have forced mercury out of everyday products: thermometers would be banned for consumer sale, other mercury-containing items like batteries and fluorescent bulbs would have to be labeled, separated from the trash, and eventually phased out unless the EPA granted an exemption. Facilities would have to monitor their emissions and report the data publicly, so residents could see what each plant was putting into the air.
analysis.who_benefits: People who eat fish from contaminated waters, pregnant women and children most exposed to mercury, and communities near coal plants, incinerators, and cement kilns. The bill's own findings cite the National Academy of Sciences estimate that 60,000 children are born each year at risk of mercury-related neurodevelopmental effects, and note that 40 states had issued fish consumption advisories. The bill would also have required public, facility-by-facility emission data, giving residents direct information about local pollution.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Fish eaters, pregnant women, children near plants

how_it_helps.text: Requires every fossil fuel-fired electric utility steam generating unit to reduce its annual mercury emissions by at least 90 percent below its baseline, with enforceable permits and quarterly monitoring reports.

Sets the same 90 percent cut for large coal- and oil-fired commercial and industrial boilers and a 95 percent cut for chlor-alkali plants and Portland cement plants, with captured mercury required to be disposed of so it cannot re-enter the environment.

Bans the sale of mercury thermometers to consumers, requires manufacturers to label mercury-containing products, and phases out mercury-containing products three years after enactment unless the EPA grants an exemption for an essential product with no reasonable alternative.

Requires public annual reporting of facility-specific mercury emission data for power plants, boilers, incinerators, chlor-alkali plants, and cement plants, and funds research and public education aimed at populations most at risk.

analysis.who_pays: Owners of coal-fired power plants, industrial boilers, chlor-alkali plants, cement plants, and waste incinerators, who would bear the cost of emission controls, monitoring, and permits. Chlor-alkali plants using the mercury cell process would face pressure to switch processes. Manufacturers of mercury-containing products would face labeling, take-back, and phase-out requirements. Some compliance costs would likely be passed to customers through electricity rates and product prices.
analysis.who_pays_short: Coal power, cement, and chemical plants

drawbacks.text: The bill mandates 90 percent reductions from each utility unit and 95 percent from chlor-alkali and cement plants, among the deepest mercury cuts ever proposed; the required control equipment and fuel switching would be expensive, and power plant compliance costs are typically recovered through electricity rates, so consumers would pay part of the bill.

The timeline is tight: EPA would have had to write regulations within 180 days and every unit would need a compliant permit within two years, leaving limited room to stagger retirements or retrofits at plants that could not meet the standard.

The bill permits emission trading only among units at a single power station, not across the power grid, which lowers flexibility and raises the overall cost of achieving the same total reduction compared with a market-wide trading program.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits run to broad, diffuse publics: fewer children exposed to a potent neurotoxin, cleaner fish, and public disclosure of who is emitting what. The costs fall on a small set of industries and, indirectly, on their customers through somewhat higher electricity and product prices. The bill does have design costs — an aggressive per-unit mandate with a short compliance clock and only site-level trading is costlier than a flexible nationwide program — but the health stakes it identifies, including the 60,000-at-risk-births estimate, are large. The bill never advanced far enough for Congress to weigh those trade-offs on the record.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, then to its Energy and Air Quality Subcommittee, and no hearing, markup, or vote was ever held before the Congress ended in January 2003.

narrative.text: Rep. Thomas Allen introduced the bill on August 2, 2001, with 27 original cosponsors, and it was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce the same day.
Two weeks later, on August 16, 2001, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Energy and Air Quality, where it remained for the rest of the 107th Congress.
No further action was ever taken; the bill never received a committee vote or a floor vote and died when the Congress ended on January 3, 2003.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Coal-fired power plants, chlor-alkali plants, cement kilns, and waste incinerators are better off: they never had to face the 90 to 95 percent mercury cuts, monitoring, and product phase-outs the bill required, avoiding control costs that would otherwise have been imposed.

sides.party_line_note: Support was overwhelmingly Democratic — 23 of the 27 cosponsors were Democrats, joined by the chamber's lone Independent and just 3 of 223 House Republicans — and with Republicans holding a 223-seat House majority and control of the committee, the bill never advanced.

industries.note: The bill would have required every coal- and oil-fired power plant to cut mercury emissions 90 percent below baseline with enforceable permits and quarterly monitoring — controls that plants avoided for years under the existing Clean Air Act framework. The cost of scrubbers and carbon injection would have been borne by plant owners and partly passed to electricity customers.

Plants using the mercury cell process — an older technology for making chlorine that vents mercury — would have faced 95 percent cuts, effectively forcing a switch to mercury-free membrane technology. Their emissions land in air and water shared with the public.
Cement kilns would have had to cut direct and fugitive mercury dust emissions by 95 percent and report emissions publicly. Cement kiln mercury settles into nearby watersheds and fish.

industries.industry: Solid waste and medical waste incinerators
industries.note: Incinerators would face new monitoring rules, tighter permit terms, and a hard emissions cap of 0.080 milligrams per cubic meter, dropping to 0.060 with mandatory control equipment if they missed it. Communities near incinerators breathe what these facilities emit.

industries.industry: Mercury-containing product manufacturers (batteries, fluorescent lamps, thermometers)
industries.note: The bill requires labeling, consumer thermometer bans, waste separation plans, and a three-year phase-out of mercury products unless the EPA grants an exemption with a take-back program. Manufacturers of mercury-free alternatives would gain a market; makers of mercury products would bear compliance and redesign costs.
